## Transforming a Complex SDP into an Equivalent Real SDP

### 1. Precise statement of the complex SDP

A complex semidefinite program (in *LMI / inequality* form) is

$$
\text{(C-SDP)}\qquad \min_{z\in\mathbb C^n}\ \operatorname{Re}(c^{*}z)
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad F(z)\succeq 0,
$$

where $c\in\mathbb C^n$, and $F:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb H_m$ is an **affine, Hermitian‑valued** map. Concretely, the most general affine map whose value is Hermitian for every $z$ is

$$
F(z)\;=\;F_{0}\;+\;\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bigl(z_{j}A_{j}+\overline{z_{j}}\,A_{j}^{*}\bigr),
\qquad F_{0}\in\mathbb H_m,\; A_{j}\in\mathbb C^{m\times m},
$$

and $\succeq 0$ means *Hermitian positive semidefinite*. The objective $\operatorname{Re}(c^{*}z)=\sum_j\bigl(\operatorname{Re}c_j\,\operatorname{Re}z_j+\operatorname{Im}c_j\,\operatorname{Im}z_j\bigr)$ is real‑linear, as required.

### 2. Decomposing Hermitian matrices into real parts

Every Hermitian $H\in\mathbb H_m$ has a unique decomposition

$$
H \;=\; R \;+\; i\,S,
\qquad R=R^{\top}\in\mathbb S_m,\quad S=-S^{\top}\in\mathbb A_m
\]

(real symmetric plus $i$ times real skew‑symmetric). Apply this to the data:

* $F_{0}=R_{0}+iS_{0}$, with $R_{0}\in\mathbb S_m$, $S_{0}\in\mathbb A_m$;
* $A_{j}=P_{j}+iQ_{j}$.

Because $F(z)$ is Hermitian for **all** $z$, the real matrix $\operatorname{Re}(z_{j}A_{j})=p_{j}P_{j}-q_{j}Q_{j}$ (where $z_{j}=p_{j}+iq_{j}$) must be symmetric for all $p_{j},q_{j}$; hence **$P_{j},Q_{j}\in\mathbb S_m$** are both real symmetric. (This is automatic from the Hermiticity of $F$; it is not an extra assumption.)

Using $z_{j}A_{j}+\overline{z_{j}}A_{j}^{*}=2\operatorname{Re}(z_{j}A_{j})=2(p_{j}P_{j}-q_{j}Q_{j})$, we obtain

$$
F(z)\;=\;\underbrace{\Bigl(R_{0}+2\sum_{j}(p_{j}P_{j}-q_{j}Q_{j})\Bigr)}_{=:\,R(p,q)\,\in\,\mathbb S_m}
\;+\; i\,\underbrace{S_{0}}_{\in\,\mathbb A_m}.
$$

So $F(z)=R(p,q)+iS_{0}$, where $R(p,q)$ is real symmetric and linear in the real variables $(p,q)$, and $S_{0}$ is a **constant** real skew‑symmetric matrix (independent of $z$).

### 3. Key lemma: Hermitian PSD $\Longleftrightarrow$ real symmetric PSD

**Lemma.** Let $X=R+iS$ with $R\in\mathbb S_m$, $S\in\mathbb A_m$ (so $X$ is Hermitian). Define the real symmetric matrix

$$
\mathcal R(X)\;:=\;\begin{pmatrix} R & -S\\[2pt] S & R\end{pmatrix}\;\in\;\mathbb S_{2m}.
$$

Then $X\succeq 0$ (Hermitian PSD) $\iff$ $\mathcal R(X)\succeq 0$ (real symmetric PSD), and moreover $\operatorname{rank}\mathcal R(X)=2\operatorname{rank}X$.

*Proof.* $\mathcal R(X)$ is symmetric because $R^{\top}=R$ and $S^{\top}=-S$:
$$
\mathcal R(X)^{\top}=\begin{pmatrix}R^{\top}&S^{\top}\\-S^{\top}&R^{\top}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}R&-S\\S&R\end{pmatrix}=\mathcal R(X).
$$

Consider the real‑linear isomorphism $\varphi:\mathbb C^{m}\to\mathbb R^{2m}$, $v=u+iw\mapsto\binom{u}{w}$. A direct computation shows $\varphi$ **intertwines** multiplication by $X$ (viewed as a real‑linear operator on $\mathbb C^{m}\cong\mathbb R^{2m}$) with multiplication by $\mathcal R(X)$:
$$
\mathcal R(X)\binom{u}{w}=\binom{Ru-Sw}{Su+Rw},\qquad
X(u+iw)=(Ru-Sw)+i(Su+Rw).
$$
Hence $\mathcal R(X)$ and $X$ (as real operators) are conjugate, so they have the same eigenvalues **with the same real multiplicities**. Since $X$ is Hermitian, its eigenvalues $\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{m}$ are real, and as a real‑linear operator each $\lambda_{k}$ appears with *twice* its complex multiplicity (the complex eigenspace $\ker(X-\lambda_{k}I)$ is a complex line $\mathbb C\,v_{k}$, which is a 2‑dimensional real subspace on which $X$ acts as $\lambda_{k}\,\mathrm{Id}$). Therefore the spectrum of $\mathcal R(X)$ is $\{\lambda_{1},\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{2},\dots,\lambda_{m},\lambda_{m}\}$. In particular every eigenvalue of $\mathcal R(X)$ is $\ge 0$ iff every eigenvalue of $X$ is $\ge 0$. $\square$

### 4. The equivalent real SDP

Apply the lemma to $F(z)=R(p,q)+iS_{0}$. The complex LMI $F(z)\succeq 0$ is equivalent to

$$
\mathcal R(F(z))\;=\;
\begin{pmatrix}
R(p,q) & -S_{0}\\[2pt]
S_{0} & R(p,q)
\end{pmatrix}\;\succeq\;0,
\qquad R(p,q)=R_{0}+2\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bigl(p_{j}P_{j}-q_{j}Q_{j}\bigr).
$$

The objective is already real‑linear in $(p,q)$:
$$
\operatorname{Re}(c^{*}z)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bigl(\operatorname{Re}(c_{j})\,p_{j}+\operatorname{Im}(c_{j})\,q_{j}\bigr).
$$

Define the real data
$$
\tilde c=(\operatorname{Re}c_{1},\dots,\operatorname{Re}c_{n},\operatorname{Im}c_{1},\dots,\operatorname{Im}c_{n})\in\mathbb R^{2n},
\quad y=(p_{1},\dots,p_{n},q_{1},\dots,q_{n})\in\mathbb R^{2n},
$$
and the constant real symmetric blocks
$$
\widetilde F_{0}=\begin{pmatrix}R_{0}&-S_{0}\\ S_{0}&R_{0}\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\widetilde F_{j}^{(p)}=2\begin{pmatrix}P_{j}&0\\0&P_{j}\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\widetilde F_{j}^{(q)}=-2\begin{pmatrix}Q_{j}&0\\0&Q_{j}\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Then the **real SDP**

$$
\text{(R-SDP)}\qquad
\min_{y\in\mathbb R^{2n}}\ \tilde c^{\top}y
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad
\widetilde F_{0}+\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bigl(p_{j}\widetilde F_{j}^{(p)}+q_{j}\widetilde F_{j}^{(q)}\bigr)\;\succeq\;0
$$

is a real semidefinite program: a real linear objective subject to a **real** symmetric LMI of size $2m\times 2m$ in real variables $y\in\mathbb R^{2n}$.

### 5. Equivalence

The map $z=p+iq\mapsto y=(p,q)$ is a bijection between feasible sets, because by the Lemma

$$
F(z)\succeq 0\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \mathcal R(F(z))\succeq 0,
$$

and the objectives coincide: $\operatorname{Re}(c^{*}z)=\tilde c^{\top}y$. Therefore

* $z^{\star}$ is optimal for (C‑SDP) $\iff$ $y^{\star}=(\operatorname{Re}z^{\star},\operatorname{Im}z^{\star})$ is optimal for (R‑SDP);
* the optimal values are equal;
* every feasible/optimal point of one program corresponds to exactly one feasible/optimal point of the other (via $z\leftrightarrow(\operatorname{Re}z,\operatorname{Im}z)$ and the inverse $y=(p,q)\mapsto z=p+iq$).

### 6. Remark on the primal (variable‑matrix) form

The same construction handles the dual/primal form $\min\{\langle C,X\rangle:\langle A_{i},X\rangle=b_{i},\;X\succeq0,\;X\in\mathbb H_{m}\}$: writing $X=R+iS$ ($R\in\mathbb S_{m},S\in\mathbb A_{m}$), the cone $X\succeq0$ becomes $\binom{R\ -S}{S\ R}\succeq0$, the real trace identity $\langle C,X\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(C_{R}R)-\operatorname{tr}(C_{I}S)$ gives a real linear objective, and each equality $\langle A_{i},X\rangle=b_{i}$ becomes $\operatorname{tr}((A_{i})_{R}R)-\operatorname{tr}((A_{i})_{I}S)=b_{i}$; the symmetry/skew constraints on $R,S$ are linear equalities on entries. This is the same realification, applied to the dual side.

---

**Conclusion.** Every complex SDP (real linear objective + complex Hermitian LMI) is converted into an equivalent real SDP by (i) splitting each complex variable $z_{j}=p_{j}+iq_{j}$ into two real variables, (ii) splitting each Hermitian data matrix into $R+iS$ (real symmetric + $i$·real skew‑symmetric), and (iii) replacing the Hermitian PSD constraint $F(z)\succeq0$ by the real symmetric PSD constraint $\begin{pmatrix}R(p,q)&-S_{0}\\ S_{0}&R(p,q)\end{pmatrix}\succeq0$ via the block embedding $\mathcal R$. The Lemma guarantees this replacement is exact (eigenvalues are preserved with doubled multiplicity), so the two programs have identical feasible sets (under $z\leftrightarrow(\operatorname{Re}z,\operatorname{Im}z)$) and identical optimal values.

## Transforming a Complex SDP into an Equivalent Real SDP

### 1. Precise statement of the complex SDP

A complex semidefinite program (in *LMI / inequality* form) is

$$
\text{(C-SDP)}\qquad \min_{z\in\mathbb C^n}\ \operatorname{Re}(c^{*}z)
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad F(z)\succeq 0,
$$

where $c\in\mathbb C^n$, and $F:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb H_m$ is an **affine, Hermitian‑valued** map. Concretely, the most general affine map whose value is Hermitian for every $z$ is

$$
F(z)\;=\;F_{0}\;+\;\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bigl(z_{j}A_{j}+\overline{z_{j}}\,A_{j}^{*}\bigr),
\qquad F_{0}\in\mathbb H_m,\; A_{j}\in\mathbb C^{m\times m},
$$

and $\succeq 0$ means *Hermitian positive semidefinite*. The objective $\operatorname{Re}(c^{*}z)=\sum_j\bigl(\operatorname{Re}c_j\,\operatorname{Re}z_j+\operatorname{Im}c_j\,\operatorname{Im}z_j\bigr)$ is real‑linear, as required.

### 2. Decomposing Hermitian matrices into real parts

Every Hermitian $H\in\mathbb H_m$ has a unique decomposition

$$
H \;=\; R \;+\; i\,S,
\qquad R=R^{\top}\in\mathbb S_m,\quad S=-S^{\top}\in\mathbb A_m
\]

(real symmetric plus $i$ times real skew‑symmetric). Apply this to the data:

* $F_{0}=R_{0}+iS_{0}$, with $R_{0}\in\mathbb S_m$, $S_{0}\in\mathbb A_m$;
* $A_{j}=P_{j}+iQ_{j}$.

Because $F(z)$ is Hermitian for **all** $z$, the real matrix $\operatorname{Re}(z_{j}A_{j})=p_{j}P_{j}-q_{j}Q_{j}$ (where $z_{j}=p_{j}+iq_{j}$) must be symmetric for all $p_{j},q_{j}$; hence **$P_{j},Q_{j}\in\mathbb S_m$** are both real symmetric. (This is automatic from the Hermiticity of $F$; it is not an extra assumption.)

Using $z_{j}A_{j}+\overline{z_{j}}A_{j}^{*}=2\operatorname{Re}(z_{j}A_{j})=2(p_{j}P_{j}-q_{j}Q_{j})$, we obtain

$$
F(z)\;=\;\underbrace{\Bigl(R_{0}+2\sum_{j}(p_{j}P_{j}-q_{j}Q_{j})\Bigr)}_{=:\,R(p,q)\,\in\,\mathbb S_m}
\;+\; i\,\underbrace{S_{0}}_{\in\,\mathbb A_m}.
$$

So $F(z)=R(p,q)+iS_{0}$, where $R(p,q)$ is real symmetric and linear in the real variables $(p,q)$, and $S_{0}$ is a **constant** real skew‑symmetric matrix (independent of $z$).

### 3. Key lemma: Hermitian PSD $\Longleftrightarrow$ real symmetric PSD

**Lemma.** Let $X=R+iS$ with $R\in\mathbb S_m$, $S\in\mathbb A_m$ (so $X$ is Hermitian). Define the real symmetric matrix

$$
\mathcal R(X)\;:=\;\begin{pmatrix} R & -S\\[2pt] S & R\end{pmatrix}\;\in\;\mathbb S_{2m}.
$$

Then $X\succeq 0$ (Hermitian PSD) $\iff$ $\mathcal R(X)\succeq 0$ (real symmetric PSD), and moreover $\operatorname{rank}\mathcal R(X)=2\operatorname{rank}X$.

*Proof.* $\mathcal R(X)$ is symmetric because $R^{\top}=R$ and $S^{\top}=-S$:
$$
\mathcal R(X)^{\top}=\begin{pmatrix}R^{\top}&S^{\top}\\-S^{\top}&R^{\top}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}R&-S\\S&R\end{pmatrix}=\mathcal R(X).
$$

Consider the real‑linear isomorphism $\varphi:\mathbb C^{m}\to\mathbb R^{2m}$, $v=u+iw\mapsto\binom{u}{w}$. A direct computation shows $\varphi$ **intertwines** multiplication by $X$ (viewed as a real‑linear operator on $\mathbb C^{m}\cong\mathbb R^{2m}$) with multiplication by $\mathcal R(X)$:
$$
\mathcal R(X)\binom{u}{w}=\binom{Ru-Sw}{Su+Rw},\qquad
X(u+iw)=(Ru-Sw)+i(Su+Rw).
$$
Hence $\mathcal R(X)$ and $X$ (as real operators) are conjugate, so they have the same eigenvalues **with the same real multiplicities**. Since $X$ is Hermitian, its eigenvalues $\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{m}$ are real, and as a real‑linear operator each $\lambda_{k}$ appears with *twice* its complex multiplicity (the complex eigenspace $\ker(X-\lambda_{k}I)$ is a complex line $\mathbb C\,v_{k}$, which is a 2‑dimensional real subspace on which $X$ acts as $\lambda_{k}\,\mathrm{Id}$). Therefore the spectrum of $\mathcal R(X)$ is $\{\lambda_{1},\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{2},\dots,\lambda_{m},\lambda_{m}\}$. In particular every eigenvalue of $\mathcal R(X)$ is $\ge 0$ iff every eigenvalue of $X$ is $\ge 0$. $\square$

### 4. The equivalent real SDP

Apply the lemma to $F(z)=R(p,q)+iS_{0}$. The complex LMI $F(z)\succeq 0$ is equivalent to

$$
\mathcal R(F(z))\;=\;
\begin{pmatrix}
R(p,q) & -S_{0}\\[2pt]
S_{0} & R(p,q)
\end{pmatrix}\;\succeq\;0,
\qquad R(p,q)=R_{0}+2\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bigl(p_{j}P_{j}-q_{j}Q_{j}\bigr).
$$

The objective is already real‑linear in $(p,q)$:
$$
\operatorname{Re}(c^{*}z)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bigl(\operatorname{Re}(c_{j})\,p_{j}+\operatorname{Im}(c_{j})\,q_{j}\bigr).
$$

Define the real data
$$
\tilde c=(\operatorname{Re}c_{1},\dots,\operatorname{Re}c_{n},\operatorname{Im}c_{1},\dots,\operatorname{Im}c_{n})\in\mathbb R^{2n},
\quad y=(p_{1},\dots,p_{n},q_{1},\dots,q_{n})\in\mathbb R^{2n},
$$
and the constant real symmetric blocks
$$
\widetilde F_{0}=\begin{pmatrix}R_{0}&-S_{0}\\ S_{0}&R_{0}\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\widetilde F_{j}^{(p)}=2\begin{pmatrix}P_{j}&0\\0&P_{j}\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\widetilde F_{j}^{(q)}=-2\begin{pmatrix}Q_{j}&0\\0&Q_{j}\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Then the **real SDP**

$$
\text{(R-SDP)}\qquad
\min_{y\in\mathbb R^{2n}}\ \tilde c^{\top}y
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad
\widetilde F_{0}+\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bigl(p_{j}\widetilde F_{j}^{(p)}+q_{j}\widetilde F_{j}^{(q)}\bigr)\;\succeq\;0
$$

is a real semidefinite program: a real linear objective subject to a **real** symmetric LMI of size $2m\times 2m$ in real variables $y\in\mathbb R^{2n}$.

### 5. Equivalence

The map $z=p+iq\mapsto y=(p,q)$ is a bijection between feasible sets, because by the Lemma

$$
F(z)\succeq 0\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \mathcal R(F(z))\succeq 0,
$$

and the objectives coincide: $\operatorname{Re}(c^{*}z)=\tilde c^{\top}y$. Therefore

* $z^{\star}$ is optimal for (C‑SDP) $\iff$ $y^{\star}=(\operatorname{Re}z^{\star},\operatorname{Im}z^{\star})$ is optimal for (R‑SDP);
* the optimal values are equal;
* every feasible/optimal point of one program corresponds to exactly one feasible/optimal point of the other (via $z\leftrightarrow(\operatorname{Re}z,\operatorname{Im}z)$ and the inverse $y=(p,q)\mapsto z=p+iq$).

### 6. Remark on the primal (variable‑matrix) form

The same construction handles the dual/primal form $\min\{\langle C,X\rangle:\langle A_{i},X\rangle=b_{i},\;X\succeq0,\;X\in\mathbb H_{m}\}$: writing $X=R+iS$ ($R\in\mathbb S_{m},S\in\mathbb A_{m}$), the cone $X\succeq0$ becomes $\binom{R\ -S}{S\ R}\succeq0$, the real trace identity $\langle C,X\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(C_{R}R)-\operatorname{tr}(C_{I}S)$ gives a real linear objective, and each equality $\langle A_{i},X\rangle=b_{i}$ becomes $\operatorname{tr}((A_{i})_{R}R)-\operatorname{tr}((A_{i})_{I}S)=b_{i}$; the symmetry/skew constraints on $R,S$ are linear equalities on entries. This is the same realification, applied to the dual side.

---

**Conclusion.** Every complex SDP (real linear objective + complex Hermitian LMI) is converted into an equivalent real SDP by (i) splitting each complex variable $z_{j}=p_{j}+iq_{j}$ into two real variables, (ii) splitting each Hermitian data matrix into $R+iS$ (real symmetric + $i$·real skew‑symmetric), and (iii) replacing the Hermitian PSD constraint $F(z)\succeq0$ by the real symmetric PSD constraint $\begin{pmatrix}R(p,q)&-S_{0}\\ S_{0}&R(p,q)\end{pmatrix}\succeq0$ via the block embedding $\mathcal R$. The Lemma guarantees this replacement is exact (eigenvalues are preserved with doubled multiplicity), so the two programs have identical feasible sets (under $z\leftrightarrow(\operatorname{Re}z,\operatorname{Im}z)$) and identical optimal values.
